_meta.purpose: Category-level guidance shown alongside a model prediction.
_meta.review_status: NOT REVIEWED BY A PLANT PATHOLOGIST. Written from general agronomic sources for a portfolio project. Every entry needs review by a qualified agronomist before this is used to advise a real grower.
_meta.no_product_names: Active ingredients and trade names are deliberately omitted. Approved products differ by country and change over time, and a wrong chemical recommendation wastes money at best and harms a crop or a person at worst. Every entry defers to a local extension officer for specific products.
sources: TNAU Agritech Portal crop management pages (general practice)

cmd.name: Cassava mosaic disease
cmd.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies and, more often, by planting infected stem cuttings. There is no cure for an infected plant.
actions: Remove and destroy visibly infected plants — do not compost them.
Never take planting cuttings from an infected field.
Check neighbouring plants; the virus spreads outward from a focus.
Manage whitefly populations if numbers are high.
prevention: Source cuttings from a certified clean supplier or a known-healthy field.
Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available.
Inspect new plantings at 4 and 8 weeks, when symptoms first appear.
cmd.note: Most spread in practice comes from cuttings rather than insects, so clean planting material matters more than spraying.

cbb.name: Cassava bacterial blight
cbb.summary: A bacterial disease spread by rain splash, infected cuttings, and contaminated tools. Severe outbreaks can kill young plants.
actions: Remove and burn affected plant material.
Disinfect cutting tools between plants.
Avoid working in the field while foliage is wet — that is when it spreads.
prevention: Use clean planting material from an unaffected field.
Rotate away from cassava for at least one season on affected land.
Clear crop debris after harvest rather than leaving it in the field.
cbb.note: Bactericides are not generally effective. Sanitation and clean cuttings are the practical controls.

cbs.name: Cassava brown leaf spot
cbs.summary: A common fungal leaf spot. Usually cosmetic on established plants and rarely worth treating on its own.
actions: Note the severity and check again in two weeks.
Treat only if it is spreading rapidly across young plants.
prevention: Space plants for airflow so leaves dry after rain.
Remove heavily affected lower leaves and crop debris.
cbs.note: Yield loss from brown leaf spot alone is usually small. If plants look poor, look for another cause as well.

healthy.name: Healthy
healthy.summary: No disease symptoms detected in this image.
actions: Continue routine monitoring, particularly at 4 and 8 weeks after planting.
prevention: Keep using clean planting material.
Watch for whitefly, which spreads mosaic disease.
healthy.note: One healthy leaf does not mean a healthy field. Check several plants across the plot.

blast.name: Rice blast
blast.summary: A serious fungal disease that can destroy a crop, especially if it reaches the neck of the panicle.
actions: Treat promptly — blast moves fast under humid conditions.
Ask your extension officer which fungicide is approved locally and when to apply.
Stop applying nitrogen until the outbreak is controlled.
Drain the field briefly if standing water is deep.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Split nitrogen applications rather than applying heavily at once.
Avoid dense planting, which keeps the canopy wet.
blast.note: Excess nitrogen is the most common driver of severe blast.

bacterial_leaf_blight.name: Bacterial leaf blight
bacterial_leaf_blight.summary: A bacterial disease causing yellow lesions from the leaf tip and margins. Spreads in standing water and through wounds.
actions: Drain the field if possible — the bacteria move in water.
Stop nitrogen applications until symptoms stop spreading.
Remove severely affected plants and weed hosts around bunds.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties, which are the main practical control.
Avoid clipping seedling tips at transplanting, which creates entry wounds.
Balance nitrogen with potassium.
bacterial_leaf_blight.note: Fungicides do not work on bacterial diseases. Water and nitrogen management are the levers that matter.

bacterial_leaf_streak.name: Bacterial leaf streak
bacterial_leaf_streak.summary: Narrow water-soaked streaks between leaf veins, later turning yellow-brown. Related to bacterial leaf blight and managed similarly.
actions: Drain the field where practical.
Reduce nitrogen until spread stops.
Remove infected debris after harvest rather than ploughing it in.
prevention: Use clean, treated seed.
Plant tolerant varieties where available.
Control weeds around bunds that host the bacteria.
bacterial_leaf_streak.note: Often confused with leaf blight in the field. Both are bacterial and both respond to the same management.

bacterial_panicle_blight.name: Bacterial panicle blight
bacterial_panicle_blight.summary: Affects the panicle rather than the leaf, causing discoloured grain and blanking. Worse in hot seasons and carried on seed.
actions: Mark affected areas and avoid saving seed from them.
Keep the field adequately watered — heat stress worsens it.
Consult your extension officer; chemical options are limited.
prevention: Use certified seed rather than saved grain.
Avoid excessive nitrogen late in the season.
Plant earlier where possible to avoid flowering during peak heat.
bacterial_panicle_blight.note: Because it is seed-borne, saving grain from an affected field carries the problem into the next season.

brown_spot.name: Brown spot
brown_spot.summary: Dark brown oval lesions on leaves. Usually a sign that the crop is under nutritional or water stress.
actions: Check soil fertility — brown spot commonly follows potassium or silicon deficiency.
Correct any water stress.
Treat with an approved fungicide only if severe and spreading.
prevention: Maintain balanced fertility rather than nitrogen alone.
Use certified seed; the fungus is seed-borne.
Avoid prolonged drying of the field during grain filling.
brown_spot.note: Treat brown spot as a symptom of stress as much as an infection. Fixing fertility usually does more than spraying.

downy_mildew.name: Downy mildew
downy_mildew.summary: Causes distorted, excessively leafy growth and poor panicle formation. Associated with flooding of young seedlings.
actions: Remove and destroy affected plants — they will not recover or yield.
Improve field drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep flooding of young seedlings.
Level fields so water does not pond in patches.
Use treated seed.
downy_mildew.note: Prolonged flooding of seedlings is the usual trigger, so drainage is the main control.

tungro.name: Rice tungro
tungro.summary: A virus complex spread by green leafhoppers. Causes yellow-orange discolouration and stunting. There is no cure for infected plants.
actions: Remove infected plants promptly to reduce the source of infection.
Check for green leafhoppers and manage them if numbers are high.
Inspect neighbouring fields — tungro spreads between plots.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Synchronise planting across neighbouring fields to break the vector cycle.
Remove volunteer rice and grassy weeds between seasons.
tungro.note: Controlling the leafhopper matters more than treating the plant, because the virus itself cannot be cured.

dead_heart.name: Dead heart (stem borer)
dead_heart.summary: The central shoot is dead and pulls out easily — caused by stem borer larvae feeding inside the tiller.
actions: Cut and destroy affected tillers; the larva is inside.
Check for egg masses on leaf tips and remove them.
Consult your extension officer before spraying — insecticide is only useful at specific stages, since the larva is protected inside the stem.
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages borer build-up.
Cut stubble low after harvest and destroy it.
Use pheromone traps to time interventions.
dead_heart.note: Once the larva is inside the stem, sprays reach it poorly. Timing and sanitation do more than chemicals.

hispa.name: Rice hispa
hispa.summary: A beetle whose adults scrape the leaf surface and whose grubs tunnel inside, leaving white streaks and blotches.
actions: Check how much leaf area is affected before deciding to act.
Clip and destroy heavily affected leaf tips, which carry the grubs.
Hand-collect adults early in the morning in small plots.
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces the soft growth hispa prefers.
Keep bunds free of grassy weeds.
Avoid dense transplanting.
hispa.note: Light damage rarely justifies spraying. Rice compensates well for moderate leaf loss.

normal.name: Healthy
normal.summary: No disease or pest symptoms detected in this image.
actions: Continue routine scouting, especially around maximum tillering and flowering.
prevention: Keep nitrogen balanced — excess drives blast, blight and several pests.
Watch for leafhoppers, which spread tungro.
normal.note: One healthy leaf does not mean a healthy field. Walk the plot and check several plants.

leaf_blight.name: Northern leaf blight
leaf_blight.summary: Long grey-green to tan cigar-shaped lesions on the leaves. Serious if it reaches the upper leaves before grain filling.
actions: Check how far up the plant lesions have reached — damage above the ear matters far more than below it.
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicides if the upper leaves are affected before tasselling.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids where available.
Rotate away from maize for a season on affected land.
Bury or remove crop residue, where the fungus overwinters.
leaf_blight.note: Lesions confined to the lower leaves late in the season usually cost little yield and may not be worth treating.

leaf_spot.name: Leaf spot
leaf_spot.summary: Small to medium lesions scattered across the leaf. Several fungal leaf spots look alike at this stage.
actions: Note the severity and re-check in one to two weeks.
Consider treatment only if lesions are spreading onto upper leaves.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue.
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
Plant at recommended spacing for airflow.
leaf_spot.note: Distinguishing between the fungal leaf spots reliably needs a trained eye or a lab. If in doubt, ask an extension officer.

streak_virus.name: Maize streak
streak_virus.summary: A virus spread by leafhoppers, producing fine pale streaks along the leaf. Infected plants do not recover.
actions: Remove infected plants, especially early in the season.
Check for leafhoppers and manage them if numbers are high.
Note where in the field infection started.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties, which is the main effective control.
Plant early and avoid staggered planting dates near an infected field.
Clear grassy weeds, which host both the virus and the vector.
streak_virus.note: Early infection costs far more yield than late infection. A plant infected before six weeks may produce nothing.

leaf_beetle.name: Leaf beetle
leaf_beetle.summary: Beetles feeding on leaf tissue, leaving holes and scraped areas.
actions: Estimate what fraction of leaf area is damaged before acting.
Hand-collect in small plots.
Consult your extension officer if damage exceeds roughly a fifth of leaf area.
prevention: Keep field margins clear of alternative host weeds.
Encourage natural predators by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
Monitor weekly during early growth, when plants are most vulnerable.
leaf_beetle.note: Maize tolerates moderate leaf loss well. Spraying for light damage costs money and kills predators.

grasshopper.name: Grasshopper
grasshopper.summary: Grasshoppers feeding on leaves, typically chewing from the margins inward.
actions: Estimate numbers per plant and the fraction of leaf area lost.
Act if populations are building rapidly or plants are young.
prevention: Manage grassy vegetation around field edges, where they breed.
Monitor field margins first — infestations usually move inward.
Encourage birds and natural predators.
grasshopper.note: Occasional grasshoppers are normal and not worth treating. Sustained high numbers on young plants are the concern.

healthy.name: Healthy
healthy.summary: No disease or pest symptoms detected in this image.
actions: Continue routine scouting, particularly before and during tasselling.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue between seasons.
Watch for leafhoppers, which spread streak virus.
healthy.note: One healthy leaf does not mean a healthy field. Check several plants across the plot.

septoria.name: Septoria leaf spot
septoria.summary: Many small circular spots with dark borders and pale centres, starting on the lower leaves and moving upward.
actions: Remove affected lower leaves and destroy them — do not compost.
Avoid wetting the foliage when watering.
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicides if it is climbing the plant.
prevention: Mulch around the base to stop soil splashing onto lower leaves.
Stake or cage plants to lift foliage off the ground.
Rotate away from tomato and related crops for two to three years.
septoria.note: It spreads upward by rain and irrigation splash, so mulch and staking prevent more than spraying cures.

leaf_blight.name: Leaf blight
leaf_blight.summary: Expanding brown lesions on leaves, often with yellowing around them. Can move quickly in warm, humid weather.
actions: Remove and destroy affected leaves and any fallen debris.
Improve airflow by pruning lower foliage and thinning crowded growth.
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicides — blight can move faster than removal alone can keep up with.
prevention: Water at the base rather than over the leaves.
Space plants for airflow.
Rotate away from tomato and potato for two to three years.
leaf_blight.note: Early and late blight are managed similarly but differ in speed. If lesions spread within days rather than weeks, treat it as urgent.

verticillium.name: Verticillium wilt
verticillium.summary: A soil-borne fungus that blocks the plant's water vessels. Yellowing often starts on lower leaves and on one side of the plant. Infected plants do not recover.
actions: Remove affected plants including as much root as possible.
Do not replant tomato or a related crop in the same spot this season.
Mark the location — the fungus persists in soil for years.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties, usually marked with a V on the seed packet.
Rotate with non-susceptible crops such as cereals for several years.
Solarise affected soil where the climate allows.
verticillium.note: Fungicides do not reach a soil-borne vascular pathogen. Resistant varieties and rotation are the only reliable controls.

leaf_curl.name: Tomato leaf curl virus
leaf_curl.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies, causing upward curling, puckering and stunted growth. There is no cure for an infected plant.
actions: Remove infected plants promptly — they will not recover and act as a source for the rest of the crop.
Check the undersides of leaves for whitefly.
Inspect neighbouring plants, since spread is usually outward from a focus.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whitefly numbers.
Control whitefly early — once the virus is in the plant it cannot be removed.
leaf_curl.note: Managing whitefly matters far more than anything applied to the plant itself.

healthy.name: Healthy
healthy.summary: No disease symptoms detected in this image.
actions: Continue routine monitoring, checking lower leaves and leaf undersides.
prevention: Water at the base to keep foliage dry.
Watch for whitefly, which spreads leaf curl virus.
healthy.note: One healthy leaf does not mean a healthy plant. Check the lower leaves, where several problems start.

_uncertain.name: Uncertain
_uncertain.summary: The model was not confident enough to name a condition.
actions: Take another photograph: fill the frame with a single affected leaf, in even light, held steady.
Photograph two or three more leaves from different plants.
If it still cannot decide, show the plant to a local extension officer.
_uncertain.note: Declining to answer is deliberate. Below its calibrated threshold the model is wrong often enough that a guess would be worse than no answer.
